content:
Touma noticed the man in the gray coat because the headache was already blooming.

That was the first warning.

The second came when the station began to acquire extra edges. The lights were too sharp. The vending machine’s hum was too loud. Every sound seemed to have something thin and hard concealed inside it.

Touma kept walking.

He was used to trouble. Trouble outside his head could usually be outrun. Trouble inside his skull came along regardless.

Ahead of him, near a service gate, the man in the gray coat had one hand wrapped around a boy’s wrist. His other hand was inside his coat.

The boy was a small-built teenager with a school bag hanging from one shoulder. The man was speaking to him quietly, with the patient efficiency of someone explaining a procedure that would go more smoothly if everyone cooperated.

People passed them. Someone looked at the gate, then at a departure board. Someone else made a small adjustment to their route.

The boy wasn’t struggling.

Touma might have kept going if he had been. Struggling would have made this an ordinary kind of trouble, with ordinary explanations. But the boy stood perfectly still, his face emptied by terror, as if even the possibility of resistance had been taken away.

Touma knew that look.

It was not gallantry. It was recognition.

He was tired. He did not want to do this.

There were six steps between them.

He took them.

“Hey.”

The man turned his head. His hand stayed inside his coat.

And Touma caught the thought.

*Keep moving. Keep the kid quiet. Finish the handoff.*

Not words spoken aloud. Something closer and uglier: the intention beneath them, running smoothly toward its conclusion.

Touma pressed against it.

The precision was the worst part. Not a blow, not a shove. A paperknife to the edge of thought.

For an instant, it felt as though he had pushed a pin through the inside of the world.

Then he unthought it.

The man’s fingers opened.

He looked down at his empty hand with mild confusion, as if he had forgotten what he had meant to pick up. Beside him, the boy stumbled, his body discovering that the force holding it upright had disappeared. His school bag swung forward. For a moment he seemed to have a private appointment with gravity.

Touma caught him by the shoulder.

For half a second, there was relief.

The wrist was free. The gate was still closed. Whatever had been about to happen had stopped.

Then the second half arrived.

Something hiccupped in Touma’s memory.

There was no dramatic tearing, no great blank opening in his mind. Just a small interruption. A missed beat.

He looked at the boy.

The face was still there. So was the terror. Touma could see every detail perfectly.

But the familiarity was gone.

He reached inward for it and found nothing to reach toward.

That was the clean, quiet cruelty of it. He could remember recognizing the boy.

He could no longer remember why.
